hints: Compare the positions of calcium (Group 2, Period 4) and cobalt (d-block) and recall how atomic mass and atomic size differ.
Think about what density depends on, mass packed into a given volume, and which metal has heavier and smaller atoms.
Think about what controls melting point in metals, the strength of metallic bonding linked to the number of delocalised electrons per atom.
walkthrough:
Picture the two metals side by side**
Calcium is a Group 2 s-block metal with relatively large atoms and only 2 outer electrons for bonding. Cobalt sits in the d-block, its atoms are smaller because the 3d electrons shield poorly so nuclear charge pulls in more strongly, and its atoms are much heavier ($A_r$ about 59 compared to 40).

Link mass and size to density**
Density is mass per unit volume. With cobalt you are packing a heavier mass into a smaller atomic volume, and the lattice packs efficiently. That is why cobalt is much denser than calcium.

Link electrons to melting point**
Melting breaks down the metallic lattice, so you must overcome attraction between cations and the sea of delocalised electrons. Calcium contributes 2 electrons per atom. Cobalt can contribute its 4s electrons plus 3d electrons, giving many more delocalised electrons and a higher charge density on the cation. Stronger attraction needs more thermal energy, so melting point is higher.

Final answer: Density of cobalt is higher than calcium. Melting point of cobalt is higher than calcium.
Density: Co has larger $A_r$ and smaller atomic radius, so heavier atoms packed into smaller volume.
Melting point: Co has stronger metallic bonding as more delocalised electrons (3d and 4s) are attracted to cations.

hints: Focus on the two essential components, what sits in the centre and what surrounds it.
walkthrough:
Build the picture of a complex**
Imagine a central $\text{Co}^{3+}$ or other transition metal ion. Around it, molecules or ions like $\text{NH}_3$, $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ or $\text{Cl}^-$ use a lone pair to bond to the metal. Those surrounding species are ligands, and the whole assembly of centre plus ligands is the complex, which may be a cation, anion or neutral molecule.
Final answer: A molecule or ion formed by a central metal atom or ion surrounded by one or more ligands.

hints: Recall what must stay the same (atoms present) and what must change (how they are joined) for structural isomers.
walkthrough:
Separate formula from structure**
Both compounds contain Co, N, H, Br, S and O in the same total numbers. What differs is connectivity, in one case $\text{Br}$ is inside the coordination sphere and $\text{SO}_4^{2-}$ is outside, in the other it is reversed. Same atoms, different structural arrangement, so structural isomers.
Final answer: Compounds with the same number and type of atoms but with a different structural formula (different arrangement of bonds).

hints: Count the ligands bonded to Co in $[\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_5\text{Br}]^{2+}$ to find the coordination number and its usual shape.
walkthrough:
Count then draw**
There are $5 \times \text{NH}_3$ plus $1 \times \text{Br}$, so coordination number is 6. Six ligands point to the corners of an octahedron to minimise repulsion. Put Co in the centre, draw four ligands in the plane (use a solid wedge for one coming out and a hashed wedge for one going back to show 3D), one up and one down. Label $\text{Br}$ on any one position and $\text{NH}_3$ on the other five.

Final answer: Octahedral 3D diagram with Co at centre, five $\text{NH}_3$ and one $\text{Br}$ arranged octahedrally (four in plane with wedge and hashed wedge bonds, one above and one below).
Shape: octahedral.

hints: Remember how a ligand attaches to a metal, which species supplies both electrons for the bond.
walkthrough:
See who gives the electrons**
Each $\text{NH}_3$ has a lone pair on N. It donates both electrons into a vacant orbital on $\text{Co}^{3+}$. A covalent bond where one atom supplies both electrons is a co-ordinate or dative covalent bond.
Final answer: Co-ordinate (dative covalent) bond.

hints: Assign charges of $\text{NH}_3$, $\text{Br}^-$ and $\text{SO}_4^{2-}$ and balance against the overall ion charge to find Co.
walkthrough:
Balance charges**
$\text{NH}_3$ is neutral. For $[\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_5\text{Br}]^{2+}$: $$x + 5(0) + (-1) = +2$$ so $x = +3$. For $[\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_5\text{SO}_4]^+$: $$x + 5(0) + (-2) = +1$$ so $x = +3$. Both contain cobalt(III).
Final answer: In $[\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_5\text{Br}]^{2+}$ oxidation number of Co = +3. In $[\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_5\text{SO}_4]^+$ oxidation number of Co = +3.

hints: Identify which ions are free in solution for each isomer, $\text{SO}_4^{2-}$ is free in the first compound and $\text{Br}^-$ is free in the second.
Recall the specific reagents for halide ions ($\text{AgNO}_3$) and for sulfate ions ($\text{Ba}^{2+}$) and that coordinated ligands do not precipitate.
walkthrough:
Spot what is free to react**
These are ionisation isomers. Only the ion outside the square brackets is free in water. So $[\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_5\text{Br}]\text{SO}_4$ releases $\text{SO}_4^{2-}$ but its $\text{Br}$ is locked to Co and will not form $\text{AgBr}$. The other isomer releases $\text{Br}^-$ but its sulfate is locked and will not form $\text{BaSO}_4$.

Apply the two classic precipitation tests**
For bromide, add $\text{HNO}_3$ then $\text{AgNO}_3$. Free $\text{Br}^-$ gives a cream precipitate: $$\text{Ag}^+(\text{aq}) + \text{Br}^-(\text{aq}) \rightarrow \text{AgBr}(\text{s})$$ For sulfate, add $\text{BaCl}_2$ or $\text{Ba}(\text{NO}_3)_2$. Free $\text{SO}_4^{2-}$ gives a white precipitate: $$\text{Ba}^{2+}(\text{aq}) + \text{SO}_4^{2-}(\text{aq}) \rightarrow \text{BaSO}_4(\text{s})$$ Each compound gives a positive result with one reagent and no precipitate with the other.

Final answer: Test 1: add acidified $\text{AgNO}_3$ (or $\text{Ag}^+$ with $\text{HNO}_3$). $[\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_5\text{SO}_4]\text{Br}$ gives cream precipitate of $\text{AgBr}$, $[\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_5\text{Br}]\text{SO}_4$ gives no reaction (no precipitate).
Test 2: add $\text{BaCl}_2$ or $\text{Ba}(\text{NO}_3)_2$ or $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ (or $\text{Ba(OH)}_2$). $[\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_5\text{Br}]\text{SO}_4$ gives white precipitate of $\text{BaSO}_4$, $[\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_5\text{SO}_4]\text{Br}$ gives no reaction.

hints: Recall that colour in transition metal complexes comes from d-d electron transitions and the size of the energy gap $\Delta E$.
Consider how changing the ligand from $\text{Br}^-$ to $\text{SO}_4^{2-}$ changes that splitting and therefore the light absorbed.
walkthrough:
Connect colour to splitting**
Colour arises when a d electron is promoted across the gap between split d orbitals. The gap $\Delta E$ is set by the ligands. $\text{Br}^-$ and $\text{SO}_4^{2-}$ (and the $\text{NH}_3$ set around them) split the d orbitals by different amounts.

Connect absorption to observed colour**
Since $\Delta E = h\nu$, a different gap means a different frequency and wavelength is absorbed from white light. The remaining wavelengths are transmitted or reflected, so the eye sees a different complementary colour for the two complexes.

Final answer: The different ligands cause a different d-orbital splitting / different $\Delta E$.
Different wavelength / frequency of light is absorbed, so different colour is transmitted / observed.

hints: Compare physical states, a solid catalyst with gaseous reactants is heterogeneous, while a catalyst in the same phase as reactants is homogeneous.
Sort the four examples by checking whether the catalyst and reactants are in the same phase or different phases.
walkthrough:
Use phase as the test**
If catalyst and reactants are in different phases it is heterogeneous, usually a solid catalyst with gaseous or aqueous reactants. If all are in the same phase it is homogeneous.

Classify the four cases**
Fe in the Haber process is solid Fe with gaseous $\text{N}_2$ and $\text{H}_2$, so heterogeneous. $\text{V}_2\text{O}_5$ in the Contact process is solid with gaseous $\text{SO}_2$ and $\text{O}_2$, so heterogeneous. $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ catalysing aqueous $\text{I}^-$ and $\text{S}_2\text{O}_8^{2-}$ is all in solution, so homogeneous. $\text{NO}_2$ catalysing gaseous oxidation of $\text{SO}_2$ is gas with gas, so homogeneous.

Final answer: Heterogeneous: Fe in the Haber process, $\text{V}_2\text{O}_5$ in the Contact process.
Homogeneous: $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ in the $\text{I}^- / \text{S}_2\text{O}_8^{2-}$ reaction, $\text{NO}_2$ in the oxidation of $\text{SO}_2$.
